Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Crowding: Crowded places, Moral Violation: People misbehaving
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Mika is a 53-year-old married man of Pacific Islander background who has spent most of his adult life in tightly controlled professional environments, first in the military and later as an airline pilot. He describes the trauma that still governs his days as a period of captivity years ago, when he was detained, interrogated, and tortured by men who kept him confined in a small locked space and brought him out unpredictably for questioning and abuse. What stays with him most clearly is not a single scene but a series of sharply fixed images: the metal door, the faces that appeared without warning, the posture of men standing too close, the sight of someone crying nearby and being punished for it. When he speaks about that time, his memory comes in flashes that he experiences as if he were looking at photographs held right in front of him. He can see details with disturbing clarity, and at times, when the memory presses in, he can also smell what was in the air then—stale sweat, dampness, the odor of the room. Those moments overtake him so intensely that he has to stop talking, look away, and steady himself before he can continue.

In the months after he was released, Mika tried to return to ordinary routines and to the disciplined identity he had always valued. Outwardly he resumed work and family life, but he found himself reacting to situations that seemed harmless to other people. Crowded places became especially difficult. In airport terminals, security lines, and packed boarding areas, he felt hemmed in and alert in a way that reminded him too much of being trapped among bodies and unable to control who came near him. He learned to arrive by back entrances when possible, to wait in quieter crew areas, and to ask colleagues to handle parts of airport transit he once would have done himself. As a pilot, he could function inside the structured environment of the cockpit, where roles were defined and space was controlled, but moving through the terminal often felt like the hardest part of the day. He watched other people constantly, scanning faces, hands, and posture for any sign that someone might turn threatening. He knew this made him seem distant and severe, yet from his point of view it felt necessary; relaxing his attention did not seem safe.

He has also become acutely unsettled by unusual silence. At home, if the house goes too quiet, he feels a rising certainty that something dangerous is about to happen. Silence does not register to him as peace but as the moment before a door opens, before footsteps approach, before harm arrives. His wife has noticed that in those moments he stops whatever he is doing and listens, his body tense, his eyes fixed. At night he repeatedly checks doors and windows, then checks them again. He describes knowing on one level that the locks are there, yet feeling unable to trust that knowledge for long. He goes from the front door to the back, then to the windows, testing handles with his hands until he gets a brief sense of relief. This routine has stretched evenings late and has become a source of strain at home, especially when his wife tells him they are safe and he cannot accept it.

Another set of moments catches him off guard because they seem to carry a moral charge as much as a sensory one. When he sees people misbehaving—someone bullying a gate agent, shoving in a line, acting cruelly or lawlessly—he feels a surge of alarm and disgust that is disproportionate even to him. He has come to believe that ordinary breaches of decency are not minor; they signal the kind of person who could do terrible things if given the chance. Crying is also difficult for him to witness. If he sees an adult crying in public, or if his wife tears up during an argument or sad conversation, he feels himself seized by the atmosphere of captivity, as though emotion itself has become dangerous. He is not indifferent to distress; what frightens him is how quickly tears pull him back toward those frozen images and the smell of that place.

Over time these patterns have narrowed his life. He avoids social gatherings that involve noise and crowding, sits where he can monitor exits, and keeps interactions brief with people he does not know. He has become more rigid at work and more withdrawn at home, not because he wants distance from others but because he is tired of feeling ambushed by his own reactions. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident in a crowded terminal after a schedule disruption. A passenger was shouting at staff, another person nearby began crying, and Mika suddenly caught the smell from his memory so vividly that he had to step away and stop himself from being overwhelmed. He was shaken by how completely the past could enter the present, even in the middle of his professional life. Coming to treatment, he says he wants to keep flying and remain present with his wife without constantly bracing for danger. What he fears most is that he will never be able to trust quiet, strangers, or even his own mind enough to feel fully back in his life.
